summary: Specifies an EAP mechanism for authentication and session key distribution using the Authentication and Key Agreement mechanism used in UMTS and CDMA2000 mobile networks. AKA uses symmetric keys, typically on a subscriber identity module. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile networks prove a phone's identity with a challenge-response system that uses a secret key held in the phone's SIM card. The Extensible Authentication Protocol is the general way many kinds of networks do that proof. This memo lets the two work together: the phone and the network run the mobile challenge-response inside EAP messages, ending with an agreed session key. It is how a phone can join a Wi-Fi network using the same credentials and infrastructure as the mobile network.

how does eap-aka authenticate a phone
subtitle: How the mobile phone world's AKA challenge-response authentication is carried inside the Extensible Authentication Protocol.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks already authenticate subscribers with AKA, a challenge-response method built on a secret key stored in the phone's SIM. Network access points using EAP had their own separate methods and could not reuse that infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-AKA packages AKA inside EAP messages, so a phone and a server prove each other's identity from a shared 128-bit key, then derive the session keys the link needs.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC from January 2006 that has been updated by RFC 5448 and RFC 9048, with EAP-AKA' and the newer EAP-AKA'11 replacing this version.

today: RFC 4187 is an Informational RFC published in January 2006. It has been updated by RFC 5448, which defines EAP-AKA', and by RFC 9048, which defines EAP-AKA'11. Those successors address weaknesses in this original method, and this RFC has no recorded obsoletion.

sections.title: Running AKA Inside EAP
sections.content:
EAP-AKA is an authentication method for the Extensible Authentication Protocol, described in RFC 3748. It is based on the Authentication and Key Agreement mechanism used by 3rd generation mobile networks: a challenge-response protocol built on a symmetric 128-bit pre-shared secret, which the subscriber and the network both hold.

In 3G networks, AKA is used both for radio network authentication and for IP multimedia service authentication, and those uses involve different identities: the radio side uses the International Mobile Subscriber Identifier (IMSI), while the IP multimedia side uses a Network Access Identifier (NAI). EAP-AKA was designed to fit this mobile infrastructure, so a network that already trusts a mobile operator's authentication centre can authenticate a subscriber over EAP-compatible links, most notably wireless local area networks. The authenticator and the EAP server are separate roles, and EAP-AKA is commonly carried between the EAP server and a AAA server.
sections.plainLanguage: Aka is the mobile network's way of proving that a phone really belongs to the subscriber named by its SIM. EAP is the general language many access networks use for the same job. This method lets the two fit together, so a phone can use its mobile identity to get onto other kinds of networks.

sections.title: Challenge, Response and Hidden Identities
sections.content:
The method rests on the same ideas as AKA. The server sends a random challenge (RAND) and an authentication token (AUTN); the peer computes a response (RES) from the challenge and its secret key, and checks that the token proves the server's own knowledge of the key. Both sides also compute a message authentication code over the exchange, so each EAP-AKA message is integrity protected.

A distinguishing feature of EAP-AKA is how it hides the subscriber's permanent identity. Because that identity never changes, revealing it in the clear would let observers track the user across networks. Instead, the peer normally answers the identity request with a temporary identity, either a pseudonym or a fast re-authentication identity, and only falls back to the permanent identity when the server asks for it, for instance because it cannot map the pseudonym. The server generates the pseudonyms and re-authentication identities and must be able to map them back to the permanent identity, which is typically derived from the IMSI. The permanent identity, when it must be used, is still protected from passive eavesdroppers by the way it is carried in the messages.

The peer and the server also maintain a counter, the Sequence Number (SQN), which guards against replaying old challenges. If the peer's counter and the server's counter disagree, the peer reports a synchronization failure and the server resynchronizes.
sections.plainLanguage: The network challenges the phone, and the phone answers with a value only the true SIM could produce, while checking that the network knows the same secret. Neither side trusts the other blindly. To stop outsiders following a subscriber around, the phone normally gives a temporary nickname rather than its real identity, and it keeps a counter to reject old, replayed challenges.

sections.title: The Exchange
sections.content:
A full authentication begins when the authenticator sends an EAP-Request/Identity and the peer replies with an EAP-Response/Identity, carrying a pseudonym or the permanent identity. The EAP server, often reached through a AAA server, then sends an EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge containing RAND, AUTN and a message authentication code. The peer verifies the token, computes RES, and returns an EAP-Response/AKA-Challenge carrying RES and its own message authentication code. On success the server sends EAP-Success.

The server can also use the identity exchange to steer the peer: it can ask for a permanent identity, for any identity, or specifically for a full authentication identity, and the peer names the type of identity it is offering. If the peer finds that the server's sequence number is out of step, it replies with AKA-Synchronization-Failure carrying an AUTS value, and the server resynchronizes and starts again. If the peer cannot verify the server's message authentication code, it replies with AKA-Authentication-Reject. Other messages cover notifications, client errors and, on a reconnection, EAP-Request/AKA-Reauthentication and EAP-Response/AKA-Reauthentication, which avoid the cost of a full AKA run when the peer holds a valid fast re-authentication identity.

When the server does not yet know which AKA variant the peer can run, the exchange may begin with an EAP-Request/AKA-Identity and an EAP-Response/AKA-Identity so the two sides agree before the challenge is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The conversation runs in a fixed order: the access network asks who is there, the phone answers with a nickname or its real identity, the server sends a challenge and a token, the phone answers, and the server accepts. Extra messages handle an out-of-step counter, a bad server signature, or reconnecting quickly without a full challenge.

sections.title: Keys from the Shared Secret
sections.content:
Both sides must end up holding the same key material, derived without ever sending it over the wire. The master key is computed as MK = SHA1(Identity | IK | CK), where IK and CK are the integrity and cipher keys that AKA itself derives from the subscriber key and the challenge. From that master key the method produces, in order, the encryption key K_encr of 128 bits, the authentication key K_aut of 128 bits, the Master Session Key of 64 bytes, the Extended Master Session Key, and a fast re-authentication master key.

K_encr protects selected attributes from eavesdroppers, K_aut protects the message authentication codes and checkcodes, and the Master Session Key is exported by EAP for use by lower layers, while the Extended Master Session Key is reserved for future use. The fast re-authentication key lets a peer reconnect later without running the full AKA calculation. Because the whole method depends on a symmetric pre-shared secret, there is no public-key exchange to attack, but also no ciphersuite negotiation: the algorithm suite is fixed by the mobile standards rather than chosen by the peers.
sections.plainLanguage: From the secret key and the challenge, both sides independently work out the same set of keys: one to encrypt protected parts, one to sign the messages, and a session key handed to the link layer. The same calculation also gives a key that makes later reconnections quicker.

sections.title: Security Claims
sections.content:
The memo states its security claims in the form EAP requires. Authentication is based on the AKA mechanism's symmetric 128-bit pre-shared secret. Mutual authentication is provided, as are integrity protection, replay protection and confidentiality of the protected payload, with the exception of method-specific success and failure indications, which can reveal whether an authentication succeeded. Key derivation is provided with 128-bit effective key strength, dictionary attack protection does not apply because there is no password to guess, and fast reconnect is supported. Ciphersuite negotiation, cryptographic binding, fragmentation and channel binding are not provided.

The document is candid about its own limitations: it points to a vulnerabilities section for the threats it cannot stop, and notes that the working group's review did not extend to validating the underlying AKA protocol or the security of the pre-shared key. The identity privacy the method offers protects the permanent identity from passive observers, but the temporary identities still let a server correlate a subscriber's sessions, and a peer that is forced to reveal its permanent identity loses that protection for that exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is honest about what it promises: it proves both sides, protects messages, stops replays, and produces strong session keys, but it does not let the two sides negotiate which algorithms to use. It also warns that its identity hiding is limited and that the underlying mobile authentication was outside its review.
